title: Computational Identification of Core Modules from Co-expression Network and GWAS Data
author: Sabik, Ackert-Bicknell, et al.
materials: Colocalization analysis is conducted to provide support for hypotheses linking individual genes from core modules with the GWAS phenotype. Colocalization analysis is conducted to evaluate whether two loci share a causal variant. In this instance, the coloc package is implemented to identify relationships between trait-associated GWAS loci and cis expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) from Gene-Tissue Expression project (GTEx), however, any relevant eQTL dataset could be used in this step (Giambartolomei et al., 2014, GTEx Consortium et al., 2017). The coloc package evaluates five different hypotheses regarding the relationship between the two associations and returns the probability of each as a value between zero and one: the H0 hypothesis, that neither association is significant, the H1/H2 hypotheses, that only one of the associations is significant, the H3 hypothesis, that both associations are significant but do not share a causal variant, and the H4 hypothesis, that the two associations are significant and share a causal variant. We are interested in identifying the pairs of eQTL and GWAS associations that have a high value of H4 (Table 2).Note: If no single module is identified as a potential core module in steps 4 and 5, the results may need to be aggregated to create a ranking, see troubleshooting, Problem 1.20.First, for the colocalization analysis, eQTL information from the GTEx consortium will need to be downloaded and filtered (GTEx Consortium et al., 2017). The data are available for download at https://gtexportal.org/home/datasets.Note: The tarball required for this analysis is 188 Gb in size. It would not be advisable to operate on this data on a laptop, though it may be possible. It is recommended that this file is downloaded directly to a remote server using the command line.>wgethttps://storage.googleapis.com/gtex_analysis_x7/single_tissue_eqtl_data/GTEx_Analysis_v7_eQTL_all_associations.tar.gzNote: It is possible to use eQTL from any source, however, the below code is designed to work with GTEx data and may need to be modified to work with other eQTL sources.21.Once the full eQTL data are acquired, the associations for each gene will need to be extracted from each tissue file. This can be accomplished using awk on the command line. These files can all be saved to a subdirectory of the downloaded github repo directory and read in as a part of the loop.>awk -F “\t” ‘$1 ∼ /ENSG###\ {print}’ .txt | awk -F “\t” ‘{ if (($3 >= lower_coord_limit) && ($3 tissue_gene_eqtl_output_file.txt>gene_files = list.files(“./data/eqtl_data/b4galnt3_snps/”)22.Furthermore, there are a few additional pieces of information required for input to coloc that have not been used in previous steps of this analysis. The sample size for each underlying GWAS or eQTL study, and the minor allele frequency (MAF) of the variants in each study are required. For the GTEx v7 eQTL studies, a key is provided with the sample sizes for each of these studies. The sample size for the GWAS study should be included in the summary statistics or associated manuscript. Additionally, the MAFs are included as part of the GTEx eQTL association table, and the frequencies of the alleles in the GWAS study are typically reported, however, the MAF is not always the reported frequency, so you may need to convert these frequencies if any are above 0.5. If MAFs are not reported, they can be sourced from the 1000 Genomes project using the LDLink tools.>gwas_coloc$MAF = ifelse(gwas_coloc$A1FREQ > 0.5, (1 – gwas_colos$A1FREQ), (gwas_coloc$A1FREQ))>tis = read_tsv(“./data/eqtl_data/tissue_key.txt”)23.With all of this data read in, a loop can now be run that reads in and formats eQTL and GWAS data and runs coloc for each file in the eQTL data folder. The results of the five hypothesis test for each eQTL/GWAS association pait are saved in a dataframe.a.First, an empty dataframe is initiated>gene_coloc_results = data.frame(matrix(NA, nrow = length(tis$Tissue), ncol = 8))b.Next, we initiate a loop that iterates over each eQTL file, reads it in, and formats it with appropriate variant IDs.>for (i in 1:length(gene_files)){ print(i) x = gene_files[i] y = nchar(gene_files[i]) -23 tissue = str_sub(x, 1, y) z = read_tsv(paste0(“./data/eqtl_data/b4galnt3_snps/”, x). col_names = FALSE)cols = c(“X2”, “X3”, “X4”, “X5”, “X6”)z$variant_id = docall(paste, c(z[cols], sep = “_”))z = z[,c(1,14,7,8,9,10,11,12,13)]colanmes(z) = c(“gene_id”, “variant_id”, “tss_distance”, “ma_samples”, “ma_count”, “maf”, “pval_nominal”, “slope”, “slope_se”)gene_snp_ids = GTExIdConvert(z$variant_id)z = merge(z, gene_snp_ids, by = “variant_id”)tissue_n = as.numeric(tis[which(tis$Tissue == tissue),2])...c.Finally, the coloc objects for the GWAS and the eQTL are formatted, coloc is run, and the results are written out into a dataframe....gene.coloc = list(pvalues=as.numeric(z$pval_nominal), N=as.numeric(tissue_n), type=‘quant’, snp=as.character(z$rs_id), MAF=as.numeric(z$maf))gwas.coloc = list(pvalues=as.numeric(gwas_coloc$P), N=142487 type=‘quant’, snp=as.character(gwas_coloc$SNP), MAF=as.numeric(gwas_coloc$MAF))coloc_x = coloc.abf(gene.coloc, gwas.coloc)gene_coloc_results[i,] = c(tissue,z$gene_id[1], coloc_x$summary[1], coloc_x$summary[2], coloc_x$summary[3], coloc_x$summary[4], coloc_x$summary[5], coloc_x$summary[6])}Table 2Example output for colocalization analysis using the coloc packageTissueGeneNsnpsPP.H0.abfPP.H1.abfPP.H2.abfPP.H3.abfPP.H4.abfAdipose_SubcutaneousENSG000001390448582 ×10−123 ×10−68 ×10−7.9993 ×10−6Adipose_Visceral_OmentumENSG000001390448585 ×10−143 ×10−62 ×10−8.9996×10−8

steps.title: Create GWAS gene list
steps.instruction: Generate a list of genes overlapping GWAS loci by processing lead SNPs, retrieving proxy SNPs, filtering, mapping to genes, and converting to mouse homologs.

substeps.instruction: Read the list of lead SNPs (significant GWAS variants) and create a table with SNP IDs and genome coordinates.
Register on the LDLink website, obtain an LDLink token (insert_personal_token), and install the LDLinkR R package.

Query each lead SNP against the 1000 Genomes Project using LDproxy_batch (e.g., LDproxy_batch(snp = bmd_snps$SNP, pop = "EUR", r2d = "r2", token = [insert_personal_token], append = TRUE)) to download proxy SNPs; choose the population (e.g., EUR) that matches the GWAS study.

Filter the proxy SNPs to retain only those with linkage‑disequilibrium R² ≥ 0.7, split the coordinate column into chromosome and position, and summarize each region to obtain start and end coordinates:

ld_regions = proxies %>% filter(r2 >= 0.7) %>% separate(col = coord, sep = ":", into = c("chr", "coord")) %>% group_by(query_snp) %>% summarize(chr = max(chr), min = as.numeric(min(coord)), max = as.numeric(max(coord)))
Download the GRCh37/hg19 Ensembl gene annotation from the UCSC Table Browser and create GenomicRanges objects for genes and GWAS regions:
Identify genes that overlap GWAS regions with findOverlaps, keep unique overlaps, and label them as "overlaps":
For GWAS regions with no overlapping gene, obtain the nearest upstream (precede) and downstream (follow) genes, label them accordingly, and keep unique entries:
Combine overlaps, precede, and follow tables:
Convert human gene symbols to mouse homologs using the MGI mouse‑human homology report (HOM_MouseHumanSequence.rpt):
gwas_mouse_hom = homology %>% filter(`HomoloGene ID` %in% gwas_gene_hom$`HomoloGene ID`) %>% filter(`NCBI Taxon ID` == 10090)

steps.title: Construct co‑expression network
steps.instruction: Build a weighted gene co‑expression network with WGCNA, save intermediate results, and annotate modules with gene symbols.

substeps.instruction: Cluster samples to detect outliers: sampleTree = hclust(dist(norm_exp_mat), method = "average"); plot(sampleTree) and optionally cut the tree using a chosen cutHeight.
Determine the soft‑thresholding power using pickSoftThreshold:
sft = pickSoftThreshold(norm_exp_mat, powerVector = powers, verbose = 5, networkType = "signed")
Select the minimum power where the scale‑free topology fit index plateaus (e.g., power = 8).
Construct modules with blockwiseModules using the chosen power and recommended parameters (minModuleSize = 20, mergeCutHeight = 0.15, signed network):

net = blockwiseModules(norm_exp_mat, power = 8, TOMType = "signed", minModuleSize = 20, networkType = "signed", reassignThreshold = 0, mergeCutHeight = 0.15, numericLabels = TRUE, pamRespectsDendro = FALSE, saveTOMs = TRUE, saveTOMFileBase = "./network/norm_exp_mat_TOM", verbose = 3)
Save key objects for later reuse:
save(sft, MEs, moduleLabels, moduleColors, geneTree, file = "./network/network.RData")
Annotate modules with Ensembl gene symbols (mouse example):

m = getBM(attributes = c("ensembl_transcript_id", "external_gene_name", "description", "chromosome_name", "start_position", "end_position"), filters = "ensembl_transcript_id", values = colnames(norm_exp_mat), mart = mm19)

steps.title: Perform gene‑ontology analysis
steps.instruction: Run GO enrichment for each module using ToppFun and save the results.

substeps.instruction: Export each module’s gene list to a CSV file (example for module 1):
Open ToppFun (ToppGene suite), paste the gene symbols from the CSV into the input box, and start the analysis.
When results appear, click “Download All” to save the full enrichment table.
Use the Bonferroni‑adjusted p‑value threshold of < 0.05 to define significant GO terms (Bonferroni is the most conservative correction).

steps.title: Test module enrichment for GWAS genes
steps.instruction: Assess each co‑expression module for over‑representation of GWAS‑derived genes using Fisher’s exact test and adjust p‑values.

substeps.instruction: Define the set of module colors to test:
For each color, retrieve the module’s gene table (e.g., get(paste0("mod_", color, "_trx_info"))) and compute the contingency table:
a = x                                 # overlap of module and GWAS list
b = 417 - a                           # GWAS list size (example) minus overlap
c = nrow(d) - a                       # module size minus overlap
e = 29255 - a - b - c                 # remaining expressed genes (example total)
ft_mod = fisher.test(matrix(c(a, b, c, e), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE), alternative = "greater")
Collect results into a summary table:
gwas_enrichment_results = data.frame(module_color = colors, p_value = NA, odds_ratio = NA)

steps.instruction: Perform partitioned heritability analysis for each module using the ldsc Python package.

Run ldsc with the prepared annotations, the processed GWAS sumstats, European SNP weights, and frequencies, using the overlap‑annot flag:
Parse the resulting .results file to identify modules with significant enrichment (e.g., Bonferroni‑adjusted p < 0.05) and rank them by enrichment.

steps.instruction: Calculate module‑membership (kME) scores for each gene and rank genes within a target module.

steps.title: Perform colocalization analysis
steps.instruction: Test whether GWAS loci and eQTL signals share causal variants using the coloc R package and GTEx v7 eQTL data.

substeps.instruction: Download the full GTEx v7 eQTL tarball (≈188 GB) to a remote server:
Extract tissue‑specific eQTL files into a directory (e.g., ./data/eqtl_data/).
Prepare GWAS summary data with sample size (N) and minor‑allele frequency (MAF). Convert allele frequencies >0.5 to MAF:
Read the GTEx tissue key file:
List all eQTL files for the target gene (example path ./data/eqtl_data/b4galnt3_snps/):
Loop over each eQTL file, format data, and run coloc:
tissue = str_sub(file, 1, nchar(file) - 23)   # extract tissue name
gene.coloc = list(pvalues = as.numeric(z$pval_nominal), N = tissue_n, type = "quant", snp = as.character(z$rs_id), MAF = as.numeric(z$maf))
gwas.coloc = list(pvalues = as.numeric(gwas_coloc$P), N = 142487, type = "quant", snp = as.character(gwas_coloc$SNP), MAF = as.numeric(gwas_coloc$MAF))
Save the coloc results table (e.g., as CSV).
Optional: Visualize coloc results with the RACER package (see RACER vignette at https://oliviasabik.github.io/RACERweb/articles/IntroToRACER.html).

steps.title: Analyze phenotypes with PhenStat
steps.instruction: Test knockout mouse phenotypes for genes of interest using IMPC data and the PhenStat R package.

substeps.instruction: Identify candidate genes from the core module (e.g., those with significant colocalization).
For each gene, go to https://www.mousephenotype.org/, search the gene name, and navigate to the gene’s phenotype page (example: B4galnt3 at https://www.mousephenotype.org/data/genes/MGI:3041155).
Download the “PhenStat‑ready raw experiment data” for the desired phenotype via the “Access the results programmatically” link.
Load the downloaded data into R:
url = "https://www.mousephenotype.org/data/exportraw?..."   # actual URL for the phenotype
dataset1 = dataset1[, c(15,16,21,26,28)]   # keep relevant columns
test = PhenList(dataset1, testGenotype = "JR29804", dataset.colname.batch = "Assay.Date", dataset.value.male = "male", dataset.value.female = "female", dataset.clean = TRUE, outputMessages = TRUE)
Run the statistical test on the dependent variable (e.g., "Value"):
View a summary of the test:
Generate a boxplot of genotype vs. value (sex‑stratified):
boxplotSexGenotype(test, depVariable = "Value", graphingName = "Bone Mineral Density", outputMessages = TRUE)
If batch effects were corrected, use the batch‑adjusted version:
Extract batch‑adjusted values (if needed) with getColumnWeightBatchAdjusted and plot with ggplot2 or another graphics package.

description: Note: Further discussion of the research questions underlying this protocol can be found in our two prior publications that leveraged this approach (Calabrese et al., 2016, Sabik et al., 2020). For example, in these publications, we explore the specificity of the module enrichments against other GWAS studies and more deeply characterize the topology of the genes in the annotated gene lists within the co-expression modules.
